title: Threats, opportunities, cause, event and effect
blurb: Describe a risk as cause, event and effect, tell threats from opportunities, and tell the risk owner from the risk action owner.
question: The finance manager is asked to arrange an insurance policy agreed as the response to a threat owned by the senior supplier. Is the finance manager the risk owner or the risk action owner?

teach.body: Formally: a risk is described by its cause (the event or situation that gives rise to it), its event (the uncertain occurrence) and its effect (the impact on objectives if it occurs). In plain English: because of X, Y might happen, which would lead to Z. Writing risks this way stops vague entries like 'supplier risk' and makes the response easier to choose.

teach.caption: The cause is usually certain already; only the event is uncertain.

head: Part
Example
rows: Only one approved crane hire firm in the region
The crane may be unavailable in week 12
Roof works delayed 3 weeks, cost up £18k

teach.body: A threat is an uncertain event that would have a negative impact on objectives; an opportunity is one that would have a positive impact. Both are risks. PRINCE2 identifies, assesses, plans for, owns and records opportunities in the same way as threats, in the same risk register. An opportunity also has a cause, an event and an effect.

teach.h: Risk owner vs risk action owner
teach.caption: The owner looks after the risk; the action owner carries out a specific action for the owner.

teach.body: A risk owner is the person assigned to take responsibility for responding to a risk: the person best placed to keep watch and make sure the response happens. A risk action owner (risk actionee) is the nominated owner of agreed actions to respond to a risk, often asked to help by the risk owner. Ownership is agreed in the implement step of the risk technique, so every risk has someone looking after it.

teach.h: Is this entry really a risk?
teach.caption: 'Our staff have little project experience' is a cause (or an issue). What might happen because of it is the risk.

teach.h: Worked scenario: a museum gallery refit
teach.body: At the Calderbrook Museum, project manager Priya Raman records: 'Because the listed building needs heritage consent (cause), approval may be delayed (event), pushing the opening back four weeks (effect).' The board agrees the senior user, Hugh Brennan, is risk owner. Hugh asks the heritage officer, Joan Mbeki, to hold early meetings with the council: Joan is the risk action owner. Priya also records an opportunity: a touring exhibition may become available, raising visitor numbers.

teach.text: Classic traps: (1) The risk OWNER responds to and manages the risk; the risk ACTION OWNER carries out an agreed action for the owner. (2) A statement of a current fact is a cause or an issue, not a full risk description. (3) Opportunities go in the risk register too.

items: Describe risks as cause, event and effect.
Cause: the situation giving rise to the risk; event: the uncertain occurrence; effect: impact on objectives.
Threat = negative; opportunity = positive; same discipline for both.
Risk owner: responsible for responding to the risk.
Risk action owner (risk actionee): owns agreed actions, often asked by the risk owner.

summary: You can now describe a risk as cause, event and effect and recognize when an entry is only a cause or an issue. You can also tell the risk owner, who is responsible for responding to a risk, from the risk action owner, who carries out agreed actions.

A.q: Which part of a risk description is the uncertain occurrence?
A.why: The risk event is the uncertain occurrence; the cause gives rise to it and the effect is the impact on objectives.

whyNot.0: The cause is the situation that gives rise to the risk and is often already certain.
whyNot.1: The effect is the impact on objectives if the event happens.
whyNot.2: The response is the action chosen to deal with the risk, not part of its description.

options: The person who carries out an agreed action for the risk
The person who maintains the risk register for the project
The person who first raised the risk with the project manager
The person assigned responsibility for responding to the risk
A.why: The risk owner is the person assigned to take responsibility for responding to a risk (manual 9.2).

whyNot.0: That is the risk action owner (risk actionee).
whyNot.1: Maintaining the register is typically project support's task.
whyNot.2: Raising a risk does not make someone its owner; ownership is assigned.

A.q: What is another name for the risk action owner?
A.why: The risk action owner is also known as the risk actionee.

whyNot.0: Sponsor is not a PRINCE2 role or risk term.
whyNot.1: The author is the person who raised the risk; that is a different register entry.
whyNot.3: Assessing is a technique step, not an alternative name for this role.

B.q: A team writes: 'Because the software vendor has announced a new release, the upgrade may be delayed, which would push go-live back by a month.' Which part is the effect?
options: The vendor has announced a new release
Go-live would be a month later
A new release is due from the vendor
B.why: The effect is the impact on objectives if the event occurs: a month's delay to go-live.

whyNot.0: The announcement is the cause, a situation that already exists.
whyNot.1: The possible delay is the uncertain event.
whyNot.3: This restates the cause, not the effect.

B.q: The executive owns a threat. She asks the procurement lead to negotiate a fixed-price clause as the agreed response. What is the procurement lead's role for this risk?
B.why: The procurement lead is the nominated owner of an agreed action asked for by the risk owner: the risk action owner.

whyNot.0: The executive remains the risk owner, responsible for responding to the risk.
whyNot.2: A change authority decides on requests for change, not risk actions.
whyNot.3: Project assurance gives the board independent confidence; it is not about carrying out risk actions.

B.q:
Which two statements about opportunities are correct?
1. They are recorded in the risk register.
2. They are uncertain events with a positive effect.
3. They are recorded in the lessons log until they occur.
4. They need no owner because they are welcome.
B.why: Opportunities are uncertain positive events (2) and are recorded with threats in the risk register (1).

whyNot.1: Statement 3 is false: an uncertain opportunity is a risk for the risk register, not a lesson.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 is false: opportunities need an owner to make sure they are pursued.
whyNot.3: Both are false: opportunities are risks with owners, recorded in the risk register.

C.q: A proposed register entry reads: 'Our team has limited experience of this software.' What is the best description of this entry, and what should be done?
options: It is a threat; record it in the risk register exactly as written
It is an opportunity; record it with a training response
It is a cause; describe the event and effect it may lead to
It is an effect; add the cause and event that would lead to it
C.why: The statement describes a current situation, so it is a cause (or an issue), not a full risk. The risk is what might happen because of it, and its effect on objectives.

whyNot.0: A current fact is not uncertain, so it is not yet a full risk description.
whyNot.1: Limited experience does not have a positive effect; it is a cause, not an opportunity.
whyNot.3: The entry is the starting situation (the cause), not the impact on objectives.

C.q: Who is responsible for responding to a risk, and who carries out a specific agreed action for them?
C.why: The risk owner is responsible for responding to the risk; the risk action owner owns agreed actions, often at the owner's request.

whyNot.0: Ownership is assigned per risk; project support maintains records rather than owning actions.
whyNot.3: Project support maintains the register; it is not the default owner of risk responses.

C.q: Why does PRINCE2 ask for risks to be written as cause, event and effect?
options: It lets the board set a separate tolerance for each cause
It shows which work package will pay for each response
It replaces the need to estimate probability and impact
It makes clear what might happen and how objectives suffer
C.why: A cause, event and effect description makes the uncertain event and its effect on objectives clear, which helps assessment and choosing responses.

whyNot.0: Risk tolerance is set for objectives at risk, not for each cause.
whyNot.1: Funding for responses comes from the risk budget, not from the description.
whyNot.2: Probability and impact are still estimated in the assess step.

reteach.title: Rain at the school fete
reteach.question: 'Rain' is not a risk description. What would a good one say?

blocks.body: Because the fete is outdoors in April (cause), heavy rain might fall on the day (event), so fewer visitors would come and takings could drop by half (effect). Now everyone can see what to do. The head teacher owns the risk; she asks the caretaker to book the hall as a back-up. The caretaker is the risk action owner.

blocks.text: The caretaker books the hall (action owner); the head teacher answers for the risk (risk owner).

explain.body: The event or situation that gives rise to the risk. It often exists already.

options: The impact on objectives if the risk occurs
The source that gives rise to the risk
The action agreed to deal with the risk
The person who identified the risk
test.why: The cause is the event or situation that gives rise to the risk.

explain.body: The impact on objectives, such as time, cost or quality, if the event happens.

test.q: In 'the launch may slip, adding £12k of hire costs', what is '£12k of hire costs'?
test.why: The extra cost is the impact on objectives, so it is the effect.

whyNot.0: The cause is the situation giving rise to the risk.
whyNot.1: The event is the possible slip.
whyNot.2: No response is described in the sentence.

explain.body: The risk owner is assigned responsibility for responding to the risk.

test.q: Which person is responsible for responding to a risk?
test.why: The risk owner is assigned to take responsibility for responding to the risk.

whyNot.1: The actionee carries out specific agreed actions.
whyNot.3: The author raised the risk but does not necessarily own it.

explain.body: Opportunities are uncertain positive events, recorded and managed like threats.

test.q: Where is an uncertain opportunity recorded?
test.why: Both threats and opportunities are recorded in the risk register.

whyNot.0: The issue register holds formal issues, which are already certain.
whyNot.1: The lessons log holds lessons, not uncertain events.
whyNot.3: That approach describes benefits reviews, not specific risks.
